extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent attorneys and applicants (India); practitioners preparing or prosecuting patent applications in pharmaceuticals, biotechnology and computer-related inventions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for examining patentability of chemical, pharmaceutical, biotechnological and computer-related inventions under the Indian Patent Act, including substantive criteria for novelty, inventive step, sufficiency of disclosure, excluded subject-matter and claim drafting guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural / positional isomers
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural isomers or positional isomers may be structurally similar or dissimilar compounds; such isomers even having close structural similarity may be considered novel over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: butane vs isobutane; ethanol vs dimethyl ether. However, when such chemical compounds have close structural similarity, similar functional similarities and enabling methods are available, an obviousness case may be made. Examine case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isomers with same empirical formula but structural differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Isomers having the same empirical formula but having structural differences may be considered novel and may not normally offend 'obviousness'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: cyclohexylstyrene is not considered prima facie obvious over prior art isohexyl styrene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stereo-isomers / enantiomers (prima facie obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stereo isomers are prima facie obvious: once a racemic compound is known, its enantiomers are obvious because a person skilled in the art knows a chiral center exists in two optically active forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Product patent may not be granted for enantiomers derived from a known racemate. But if a new compound is claimed for the first time in its optically active pure form, a product patent may be granted. Example: (S)-enantiomer claimed where prior art disclosed the racemate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homologues (structural similarity and inventive step)
rubrics_metrics.description: Homologues normally display add-on property, are structurally similar and may lack inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be examined case-by-case; counterexamples exist where a homologous/related compound/process was held non-obvious (e.g., polymerisation using a sterically hindered amine over prior art of unhindered amines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art need not be true homologs or isomers to show obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art structures need not be true homologs or isomers to render claimed structurally similar compounds prima facie obvious if the similarity of structure and properties is sufficiently close.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: heterocyclic carbamoyloxmino pesticidal compounds where ring atom spacing differences still led court to find one skilled person motivated to make claimed compounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polymorphs (product vs process patentability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some compounds crystallize in diverse polymorphic forms; such forms can be deemed within the prior art and therefore not patentable as product claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A process patent may be allowed for a new polymorph if the polymorph is prepared by a novel process involving inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polymorphs of therapeutically active ingredients (inevitable obtainment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Polymorphic forms of therapeutically active ingredients may be deemed within prior art and non-patentable if they were inevitably obtained following the process of the basic patent on the active ingredient or were covered by a previous product patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether polymorph is inherently disclosed or inevitably obtained by earlier process/product claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metabolites (non-patentability when inevitably formed in vivo)
rubrics_metrics.description: A metabolite is unpatentable since giving the drug to a patient naturally and inevitably results in formation of that metabolite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Types of metabolites (active from inactive precursors, active with different mechanism, contributing to duration, antagonistic) are described, but the key patentability rule is inevitability of formation in vivo undermines patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prodrugs (case-by-case patentability; marked improvement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prodrugs are inactive compounds that produce an active ingredient when metabolized; prodrugs and metabolites are interlinked and their patentability must be decided on merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the existing patent covers the prodrug; prodrugs may be patentable if there is a marked improvement over the primary drug.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydrates, salts and routinely prepared derivatives (prima facie lack inventive step)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hydrates, acid addition salts and other derivatives which are routinely prepared prima facie lack inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, if there is a long-standing problem (e.g., stability, absorption) and difficulty in preparing derivatives, patentability of such a process may be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purification of known materials (non-patentable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere purification of known material does not result in patentable subject matter due to lack of novelty and inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether purification yields new properties or unexpected technical effect; mere improved purity generally insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pharmaceutical compositions — synergistic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Pharmaceutical compositions other than mere admixtures that have a synergistic effect may normally be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should show more than aggregation of properties; evidence of synergistic effect and technical contribution recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pharmaceutical compositions — new dosages/forms (limited patentability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Known pharmaceutical compositions in different new dosages and different forms (capsules, tablets, syrups, suspensions etc.) are not patentable under sections 2(1)(j), 3(d) and 3(e) of the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changing form or dosage without inventive technical contribution is not sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: New therapeutic use of known substance (normally not patentable)
rubrics_metrics.description: New use of a known substance or its new use in a pharmaceutical composition is not normally patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrable inventive step/technical contribution beyond mere discovery of new use required; many jurisdictions limit 'second medical use' claims—follow statutory provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of using pharmaceutical compositions (excluded)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any method of using pharmaceutical composition is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural/treatment methods directed to medical use are excluded; consider claim drafting alternatives (e.g., composition or Swiss-type/second medical use claims where permitted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Biotechnological inventions — natural living entities excluded
rubrics_metrics.description: Living entities of natural origin (animals, plants, human beings including parts thereof, plant varieties, seeds, species, genes and micro-organisms) are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also applies to any process of manufacture or production relating to such living entities (not patentable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of treatment of human or animal body (excluded)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any method of treatment such as medicinal, surgical, curative, prophylactic, diagnostic and therapeutic of human beings or animals are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims directed to clinical/therapeutic methods are excluded from patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transgenic animals/plants (living entities of artificial origin) — exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Any living entity of artificial origin such as transgenic animals and plants, any part thereof are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish from other engineered biological materials; check if other provisions or specific exceptions apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Living entities of artificial origin such as micro-organisms and vaccines (patentable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Living entities of artificial origin such as micro-organisms, vaccines are considered patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentability depends on substantive human intervention and meeting novelty/inventive step/sufficiency requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological materials like organs, tissues, cells, viruses (excluded under Section 3(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Biological materials such as organs, tissues, cells, viruses etc. and processes of preparing thereof are not patentable under Section 3(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully map claimed subject-matter to statutory wording; recombinant/engineered materials may be treated differently if produced by human intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recombinant DNA, plasmids and processes (patentable with human intervention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Biological material such as recombinant DNA, plasmids and processes of manufacturing thereof are patentable provided they are produced by substantive human intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sufficiency of disclosure and deposit requirements apply; demonstrate technical contribution and industrial applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gene/DNA sequences without disclosed function (lack inventive step/industrial application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gene sequences, DNA sequences without having disclosed their functions are not patentable for lack of inventive step and industrial application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional disclosure and demonstrated utility/industrial applicability needed to support patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processes relating to micro-organisms or producing chemical substances using micro-organisms (patentable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes relating to micro-organisms or producing chemical substances using such micro-organisms are patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure processes involve human technical contribution, novelty, inventive step and sufficient disclosure (e.g., deposited strains if required).

rubrics_metrics.name: Essentially biological processes for plants and animals (excluded)
rubrics_metrics.description: Essentially biological processes for the production of plants and animals such as methods of crossing or breeding are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical, non-natural processes (e.g., specific laboratory steps) may be patentable—distinguish 'essentially biological' from technical processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public order/morality exclusion for biological inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Any biological material and method of making the same which is capable of causing serious prejudice to human, animal or plant lives or health or to the environment, or contrary to public order and morality, are not patentable (e.g., terminator gene technology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ethical, environmental and public order implications; processes like cloning, germ-line modification, uses of embryos are explicitly excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processes for cloning, germ-line modification, genetic identity alteration, embryo uses (excluded)
rubrics_metrics.description: Processes for cloning human beings or animals, processes for modifying the germ line, genetic identity of human beings or animals, uses of human or animal embryos for any purpose are not patentable as they are against public order and morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims touching these areas should be refused on public order/morality grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of source/geographical origin of biological material in specification
rubrics_metrics.description: In case of use of biological material in the invention disclosed, the source or geographical origin of such material is required to be mentioned in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure applicants include provenance information to support novelty/ethical/sovereignty considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposit requirement for new biological materials (Budapest Treaty / IDA)
rubrics_metrics.description: In case of use of new biological materials in the invention disclosed in the patent application, such materials are required to be deposited in any of the International Depositary Authorities (IDA) recognized under the Budapest Treaty on or before filing of the application to supplement the description for sufficiency of disclosure; reference of such deposit to be made in the patent specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to deposit or reference deposit may lead to insufficiency of disclosure objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traditional knowledge / aggregation of known components (non-patentable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any invention which in effect is traditional knowledge or which is an aggregation or duplication of known properties of traditionally known components is not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine prior art including traditional knowledge databases; mere aggregation without inventive technical contribution is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of invention (Section 2(1)(j)): novelty, inventive step, industrial application
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must be a new product or process involving an inventive step and capable of industrial application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All claims must be assessed against novelty, inventive step (non-obviousness) and industrial applicability criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excluded subject-matter for computer-related inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: A mathematical or business method or a computer program per se or algorithms is not patentable; also excluded are literary, dramatic, musical or artistic works, mere schemes/rules/methods of performing mental acts or presentation of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computer-related claims must avoid being framed as mere algorithms, business methods, mental acts or presentations of information; focus on technical effect/technical contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer program product claims (storage medium) treated as software per se — not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims like 'computer program product in computer readable medium' are treated as relating to software per se irrespective of the storage medium and are not held patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encoding instructions on a particular medium does not change the exclusion; seek hardware-software combination/technical implementation to show patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embedded systems and hardware+software combinations (potentially patentable)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention consisting of hardware along with software or computer program in order to perform the function of the hardware may be considered patentable (e.g., embedded systems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show how software produces a technical advancement in the hardware or an interaction producing a new technical result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure for computer-related inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the application relates only to a machine (hardware), the best mode of operation must be described with suitable illustrations; for process-related inventions the necessary sequence of steps should be clearly described to distinguish the invention from prior art with the help of flowcharts; source/pseudo/object codes may be incorporated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide enough technical details to enable a skilled person to carry out the invention; include flowcharts, hardware descriptions and, where appropriate, code snippets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art analysis for computer-related inventions (technological features vs intellectual content)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential to analyse the invention in light of prior art to identify the contribution to the art and hence determine whether the advancement resides in, or necessarily includes, technological features or is solely intellectual in its content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hardware implementation performing a novel function is not patentable if that particular hardware system is known or is obvious irrespective of the function performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categories of claims in computer inventions (method/process, apparatus/system, computer program product)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications may fall under method/process, apparatus/system or computer program product claims; different issues apply to each category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should look at specific aspects per category (see subsequent criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method/process claims for computer-related inventions (technical effect required)
rubrics_metrics.description: The method claim should clearly define the steps involved; it should have a technical effect and solve a technical problem. Claims should incorporate details regarding mode of implementation via hardware or software for clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process/method claims should contain a hardware or machine limitation and be defined in relation to particular hardware components to avoid being 'software per se'. Processes carried out under control of a program can be allowable if tied to specific hardware/technical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparatus/system claims for computer-related inventions (constructional hardware features)
rubrics_metrics.description: The apparatus claim should clearly define the inventive constructional hardware features and should incorporate a 'process limitation' defining the specific application (not general application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that merely recite functional means corresponding to steps of an excluded method may be rejected. A novel solution involving internal computer operations or particular hardware interactions that produce a technical effect can be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer program product claims (not allowable) and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims relating to software program products (program on a computer-readable storage medium) are not allowable as they are software per se; claiming instructions encoded on a medium does not affect the issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, if the new feature requires specific hardware adoption or the invention consists of hardware with software to perform hardware function (embedded systems), patentability may be possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine technical contribution / 'technical character' in software-related inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is necessary for the applicant to describe the 'technical contribution' to the prior art when the invention involves software. The technical problem which needs to be solved should be sufficiently described and how the hardware is controlled by the software to overcome the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'technical character' of the invention should be brought out clearly in the claims and specification; focus examination on whether claimed features produce a new technical effect or improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency and best mode for hardware vs software claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Best mode must be described for hardware; for software-implemented processes provide sequence of steps and flowcharts; source/pseudo/object codes may be included to support sufficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose best mode or necessary implementation details may lead to insufficiency objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples and precedents guiding allowability (jurisprudence-informed assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The guidelines summarise case law (Diamond v. Diehr, Vicom, Parker v. Flook, Gottschalk v. Benson, EPO/TBA cases) illustrating when software-related inventions were allowed or refused based on technical contribution and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these precedents to assess whether claimed subject-matter is a mere algorithm/mental act/business method or whether it provides a technical solution implemented via hardware/software interaction.
